content: The Ediacaran Period, named after the Ediacara Hills in South Australia, represents the final geological period of the Neoproterozoic Era, occurring just before the Cambrian Period of the Paleozoic Era. Its designation as an official geological period was ratified by the International Union of Geological Sciences (IUGS) in March 2004 and formally announced on May 13, 2004. This marked the first declaration of a new geological period in 120 years. The type section for the Ediacaran Period is located in the Flinders Ranges of South Australia. While it overlaps with the previously proposed Vendian Period, the Ediacaran is shorter in duration. The beginning of the Ediacaran Period is not defined by a change in the fossil record, as is typical for later periods. Instead, it is marked by the base of a chemically distinct carbonate layer known as a cap carbonate. This layer, which overlays glacial deposits, signifies a sudden climatic shift at the end of an ice age. The cap carbonate is characterized by an unusual depletion of carbon-13 (¹³C) and is thought by many scientists to have a global extent, though this interpretation remains controversial. Precise dating of the Ediacaran Period at its type section in South Australia has not been possible. Consequently, the age range of 635 to 542 million years ago is based on correlations with other regions where dating has been achieved. The base age of approximately 635 million years is derived from uranium-lead (U-Pb) isochron dating of cap carbonates in Namibia. This assumes that cap carbonates worldwide are synchronous and that the correct layers have been correlated between Australia and Namibia. However, this assumption is debated, as some scientists have tentatively correlated glacial rocks in Tasmania, dated to about 580 million years ago, with those beneath the Ediacaran rocks in the Flinders Ranges. The upper boundary of the Ediacaran Period coincides with the widely recognized base of the Cambrian Period. The fossil record of animals from the Ediacaran Period is sparse, likely because animals had not yet evolved hard shells, which facilitate fossilization. The Ediacaran biota includes the oldest confirmed multicellular organisms. The most common forms resemble segmented worms, fronds, disks, or immobile sacs. These organisms bear little resemblance to modern life forms, and their relationship to the later life forms of the Cambrian explosion is challenging to interpret. Over 100 genera have been described from this period, with well-known examples including Arkarua, Charnia, Dickinsonia, Ediacaria, Marywadea, Onega, Pteridinium, and Yorgia.
